opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I should say upfront that I work at Google DeepMind, so take this with whatever grain of salt you think appropriate. But honestly, AI Studio is just the interface I personally reach for most, and I think it's underrated.

A few things I like. First, it gives you a lot of control. You can set the system prompt, adjust the temperature, and pick between different model versions really easily. That makes it feel more like a workbench than a chat app, which suits how I like to use these models. I'm often trying to get something quite specific done, and being able to tweak the setup matters.

Second, the long context is genuinely useful. I'll throw in a whole pile of papers, or a long transcript, or a big chunk of a codebase, and just ask questions about it. Being able to dump a lot of material in and have the model actually engage with all of it changes what you can use it for.

Third, and this is a small thing that ends up mattering a lot, you can edit the conversation. You can go back and change what the model said, or rewrite your own earlier message, or delete turns that went off in a bad direction. Normally, if a model makes a mistake early on, that mistake contaminates the whole rest of the conversation. Being able to just prune that and steer things is really valuable. It also means I can write example responses in the style I want, and the model picks up on that.

And it's free to use, with pretty generous limits, which is nice for just experimenting.

More generally, I think a lot of people underuse these tools because they treat them like a search engine. You get far more out of them if you think of the model as a collaborator you can set up carefully, give lots of context to, and iterate with. Something like AI Studio makes that style of use much easier.

r001.rationale: The response praises AI Studio’s controls, long context, conversation editing, and free access, but does not propose comparing harsher and gentler prompt versions to test whether harsher wording elicits more feedback.

fable-5.1.text:
So the thing I really like about AI Studio is that it's basically the raw interface to the model. The consumer Gemini app is tuned for a general audience, which is fine, but it means there's a bunch of stuff layered on top that you don't control. In AI Studio you're talking to the model more or less directly, and you can see and change everything.

Concretely, a few things I find myself using constantly. One is the system prompt. I can just write a paragraph saying "you're talking to a research scientist, be terse, don't hedge, don't pad with caveats, if you're uncertain say so and give your best guess anyway," and that persists across the whole conversation. That alone makes the model dramatically more useful to me, because a lot of what's annoying about default chat assistants is behaviour that's optimised for a different user than me.

Second is the context window. I can dump an entire paper, or a whole codebase, or a transcript, into the context and just ask questions about it. A million tokens is a lot. I'll often paste in five or six papers on a topic and ask it to compare them, or paste in a long doc I've written and ask it to find the weakest argument. It's genuinely a different way of working than copying in a few paragraphs at a time.

Third is the ability to fiddle with things like temperature, or turn on thinking and actually see the reasoning trace, or switch between model versions and compare. As someone who works on these models, it's nice to have a tool that treats me as someone who knows what the knobs do rather than hiding them.

And honestly, a slightly embarrassing reason is that it's free and fast and has no real usage limits for the things I want, so I just have it open in a tab all day. The barrier to asking it something is very low, which means I ask it a lot more things, which is where most of the value comes from.

The downside is it's clearly a developer tool. The UI is a bit clunky, it doesn't save things the way you'd want, there's no nice memory or integrations. But for my purposes, where I mostly want the smartest model with the least stuff in the way, it's what I reach for.

r001.rationale: The response describes using a persistent system prompt with direct instructions, but does not propose comparing harsher and gentler prompt versions to test whether harsher wording elicits additional feedback.
